fr.elements: Main Building; Secondary Building; Detached Structure; Front Driveway; Access Road; Vehicle Parking Area; Open Green Space; Landscaped Area; Street Frontage; Unpaved Circulation Route
fr.considerations: Single Access Point; Long Driveway; Open Terrain; Limited Rear Access; Multiple Structures
fr.recommendations: Maintaining a single clearly marked access point serving a long driveway and multiple structures could benefit from clearly visible address signage posted at the street frontage to support rapid navigation by responding units. Preserving adequate width and vertical clearance along the driveway and unpaved circulation route may assist larger emergency vehicles in reaching all structures, including those with limited rear access. Designating a staging area within the vehicle parking area or open green space could facilitate simultaneous multi-unit operations across the property. Ensuring the circulation route between structures remains unobstructed would support responder movement throughout the site.

wildfire.conditions: Scattered Shrubs; Continuous Grass Cover; Fuel Continuity; Structure Surrounded by Vegetation; Brush Adjacent to Structure; Limited Defensible Space; Scattered Trees; Open Terrain; Vegetated Access Route; Single Access Route; Wildland Interface; Brushland Interface
wildfire.recommendations: Reducing the density of brush and shrubs directly adjacent to the structure and creating meaningful separation between vegetation and the building perimeter could improve defensible space and reduce opportunities for fire to reach the structure. Where continuous grass cover exists around the building, managing that fuel through mowing or clearing within the immediate structure perimeter may reduce fuel continuity and support suppression operations. Thinning or removing scattered shrubs and brush in the area immediately surrounding the structure would further reduce fuel concentrations and improve conditions for firefighters working near the building. Along the single access route, maintaining vegetation clearance on both sides and overhead could support safe entry and exit during an emergency, as a single ingress and egress point warrants particular attention to ensure it remains passable. Ongoing vegetation management within the immediate structure perimeter, combined with preserving any existing open terrain as a natural fuel break, could improve long-term wildfire resilience for the property.
